results.title: Derivative Pricing using Quantum Signal Processing
results.abstract_summary: The paper proposes using Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) to encode derivative payoffs directly into quantum amplitudes, avoiding costly quantum arithmetic in the payoff calculation step. It develops implementations of the required unitaries, applies the approach to common contracts (e.g., European calls and autocallables), and provides resource estimates showing substantial reductions in T-gates and logical qubits compared to prior methods.
results.methodology_description: This preprint develops and evaluates a technique to encode derivative payoffs directly into quantum amplitudes using Quantum Signal Processing (QSP), avoiding costly coherent quantum arithmetic. Methodologically the authors: (1) formulate the problem in the standard quantum derivative-pricing pipeline (reparameterization to load multivariate normals, payoff encoding, amplitude estimation); (2) design a new Usqrt unitary that, via a comparator and uniform superposition, encodes sqrt(x) into an ancilla amplitude and thus enables composition with QSP polynomials; (3) construct polynomial approximations P(x) (even/odd Chebyshev-based expansions found via an optimization/minimax routine) that approximate the target payoff-transformation on the domain [0,1]; (4) compute QSP phase factors (using available toolkits) and explicitly construct the QSP circuit U_{phi} that applies P to the singular value/g(x) created by Usqrt; (5) integrate this QSP-based payoff implementation into the reparameterization pricing circuit (assets a=3, T=20 timesteps) and use Iterative Quantum Amplitude Estimation to obtain end-to-end resource estimates to a specified accuracy; (6) implement the circuits and resource counting in Q# (extending prior Q# work) and analyze Clifford+T decompositions (Toffoli/T-gate accounting, ripple-carry comparator costs) to produce T-count, T-depth and logical qubit estimates and to compare against a baseline arithmetic-based approach from prior work. The approach is demonstrated numerically with chosen fixed-point encodings and target tolerances (examples: (n,p)=(15,5), polynomial degree d=20, target payoff error ϵ_p=1e-3). The preprint reports circuit constructions, polynomial approximation procedures, and resource estimates (T-count/T-depth/qubits/required logical T-gate rate), and compares Usqrt-driven QSP, Usin-driven QSP, and an arithmetic baseline.
algorithms_used: Clifford+T decomposition (Toffoli decomposition for resource accounting)
results.experimental_setup: All experiments are numerical/circuit-resource estimates implemented in Q# and analytic gate-count/decomposition accounting (Clifford+T model). No real QPU runs. The authors construct and count explicit circuits (Usqrt, QSP interleaves, comparators, arithmetic blocks for baseline) and use Iterative QAE to obtain end-to-end resource totals. Polynomial approximations and QSP phase-factor computations rely on Chebyshev-based optimization (as in Ref. [33]) and available QSP libraries.
results.dataset_used: No empirical financial dataset is used. Pricing experiments assume simulated/specified model parameters: geometric Brownian motion for asset paths (reparameterization approach), multivariate normal log-returns N(µ,Σ) with parameters taken conceptually from market history (not a concrete dataset). The numerical case study uses a = 3 assets and T = 20 timesteps.
results.experiment_input: Synthetic quantum-encoded distributions derived from the reparameterization method: independent standard normals loaded into a·T quantum registers then transformed to multivariate normal N(µ,Σ) for asset log-returns. Fixed-point encoding parameters used in examples: (n,p) = (15,5), so N = 2^n, r_T ∈ [−R,R] with R = 25 and shift s = R. Pricing instances: European call / autocallable option scenarios with S0,K values chosen in examples (e.g. S0 = K = 100 for illustrative polynomial plots). The input is therefore simulated paths specified by model parameters (a=3, T=20) rather than an empirical dataset.
results.experiment_process: 1) Prepare independent standard normals in a·T registers and apply the reparameterization circuit to obtain the multivariate normal N(µ,Σ) over log-returns. 2) Evaluate logical payoff trigger conditions (comparators, Toffoli/CNOT logic) into ancilla qubits to identify binary payoffs and barrier conditions. 3) For the relevant register (e.g. r_T), add shift s to make values non-negative and represent in fixed-point; apply the comparator-based Usqrt construction (uniform superposition + binary comparator C) to encode √x into an ancilla amplitude. 4) Build a polynomial P(x) (Chebyshev-based, degree chosen to meet target error) approximating the target amplitude-transform (e.g. functions of the form sqrt(1−(K_T − e^{x·scale})) or compositions described in the text). 5) Construct the QSP circuit U_{phi} (sequence of U and U† interleaved with projector-controlled Z-rotations) with phase factors obtained numerically to implement P(g(x)). 6) Apply the QSP-driven payoff encoding in place of arithmetic exponentiation and payoff arithmetic, and then run Iterative QAE to estimate the target amplitude to accuracy ϵ (examples use ϵ = 2×10^{-3} overall and ϵ_p = 10^{-3} for payoff accuracy) at confidence 1−α = 0.68. 7) Use Q# implementations and Clifford+T accounting assumptions (Toffoli decomposition, T-depth/ T-count models) to compute T-depth, T-count and logical qubit resource numbers. Key chosen parameters reported: polynomial degree d = 20, (n,p) = (15,5), a = 3 assets, T = 20 timesteps, target payoff error ϵ_p = 1e-3.
results.experiment_output: Reported quantitative resource metrics and comparisons: - Q-operator (driving amplitude estimation) resource table: Arithmetic baseline (from Ref. [9]): T-depth 36k, T-count 6.6M, logical qubits 19.2k. QSP (this work) Usin: T-depth 75k, T-count 605k, qubits 4.7k. QSP Usqrt: T-depth 7.8k, T-count 414k, qubits 4.7k. - End-to-end (Iterative QAE) for Usqrt-QSP example: logical qubits 4.7k, total T-depth ≈ 4.5×10^7, T-count ≈ 2.4×10^9, required logical T-gate rate ≈ 45 MHz to match 1s classical runtime assumption. Comparisons show ≈16× reduction in T-count and ≈4× reduction in logical qubits vs arithmetic baseline, and estimated reduction in required logical clock rate by factor ≈5×. Metrics reported: T-depth, T-count, logical qubit count, and implied T-gate rate; baseline comparisons against prior arithmetic/look-up-table based methods are provided.
results.hardware_details: No QPU experiments. Circuit construction and resource accounting performed in Q# (Microsoft Q# / QDK) and analyzed in the logical Clifford+T model. Assumptions include Toffoli->T decompositions (with ancilla-assisted T decompositions), ripple-carry comparator implementations for Usqrt, and T-depth models for rotation synthesis (Ross & Selinger results used for Ry decomposition cost estimates). No noise model or real-device transpilation was applied; resource estimates are logical (fault-tolerant) counts.
results.reproducibility_notes: Partial: the paper describes circuit constructions, parameter choices (n,p,d,a,T,ϵ), and the polynomial-construction/optimization method (Chebyshev basis + minimax optimization) and references open toolkits (QSPPACK, pyqsp). The authors state they extended a Q# implementation from prior work but do not provide a public code link in the manuscript; phase-factor computations and exact Q# code are not included in the text. Thus the experiments are reproducible in principle given access to Q# and QSP toolkits and by following the provided parameters, but full replication would require re-implementation of the Q# circuits and polynomial-phase-factor generation (not all low-level details or a code repository are supplied).
key_findings: [supported] Quantum Signal Processing (QSP) can encode derivative payoffs directly into quantum amplitudes, removing the need for coherent quantum arithmetic in the payoff component of derivative pricing circuits.

[supported] For the autocallable derivative benchmark (a = 3 assets, T = 20 timesteps, target amplitude error ϵp = 10^-3), the Usqrt-based QSP implementation reduces total T-count by ≈16x and logical qubit count by ≈4x compared to the reference arithmetic (lookup-table + arithmetic) approach.

[supported] Using the authors' resource estimates, the Usqrt-QSP method requires ≈4.7k logical qubits, total T-depth ≈4.5×10^7 and T-count ≈2.4×10^9 to reach the target accuracy for the benchmark problem.

[supported] Based on the resource estimates and assuming classical pricing in 1 second, a quantum processor would need to execute T-gates at ≈45 MHz to match classical performance for the Usqrt-QSP approach (compared to 207 MHz for the arithmetic approach and 430 MHz for Usin-QSP).

[supported] The QSP construction driven by the 'Usqrt' unitary (encoding √x via a comparator + uniform superposition) has much lower T-depth than the Usin-driven construction because Usin requires many controlled-Ry rotations that are expensive in T-depth when synthesized to Clifford+T.

[supported] A polynomial of degree d = 20 (constructed via an optimization-based Chebyshev combination) suffices to approximate the target payoff-related function to max error ≤10^-3 for the autocallable payoff instance considered.

[supported] Quantitative resource comparison table (authors' Q#-based estimates) shows: Arithmetic approach T-depth 36k, T-count 6.6M, qubits 19.2k; Usin-QSP T-depth 75k, T-count 605k, qubits 4.7k; Usqrt-QSP T-depth 7.8k, T-count 414k, qubits 4.7k.

[supported] The QSP approach trades the ability to implement arbitrary digital functions for direct amplitude transformations on the interval [0,1]; this restriction is workable for many common derivative payoffs and yields resource savings.

[speculative] The authors assert that similar QSP techniques could be applied beyond payoff encoding (e.g., to state preparation or other subroutines) to reduce resources more broadly; this is proposed but not demonstrated here for other components.
[supported] The authors identify a clear limitation: current single-variable QSP handles only scalar functions; multivariable QSP (M-QSP) could extend applicability but requires further research.
results.results_summary: The paper introduces a QSP-based method to encode derivative payoffs directly into quantum amplitudes, eliminating the costly coherent quantum arithmetic normally used in the payoff operator. Using explicit circuit constructions and Q# resource estimation for an autocallable benchmark (3 assets, 20 timesteps, target amplitude error 10^-3), the authors show large resource reductions: up to ≈16× fewer T-gates and ≈4× fewer logical qubits relative to a recent arithmetic + lookup-table approach. They demonstrate that an Usqrt-driven QSP construction is particularly efficient (d = 20 polynomial approximation was sufficient for the target error) and estimate that achieving quantum parity with a classical 1s pricing would require ≈4.7k logical qubits and a device able to perform ≈2.4×10^9 T-gates at ≈45 MHz. The manuscript also discusses limitations (single-variable functions) and potential extensions such as multivariable QSP.
performance_claims: ≈16× reduction in total T-count (6.6M → 414k) for the autocallable benchmark when comparing arithmetic approach to Usqrt-QSP
≈4× reduction in logical qubits (19.2k → 4.7k) for the same benchmark
Usqrt-QSP resources: ≈4.7k logical qubits, T-depth ≈4.5×10^7, T-count ≈2.4×10^9 to achieve target amplitude error 10^-3
Required T-gate execution rate to match classical 1s pricing: ≈45 MHz (Usqrt-QSP), compared to 207 MHz (arithmetic) and 430 MHz (Usin-QSP)
Polynomial degree d = 20 suffices to approximate the target payoff function to max error ≤10^-3 in the considered instance
Reported Q operator resource comparisons: Arithmetic T-depth 36k / T-count 6.6M / qubits 19.2k; Usin-QSP T-depth 75k / T-count 605k / qubits 4.7k; Usqrt-QSP T-depth 7.8k / T-count 414k / qubits 4.7k
results.quantum_advantage_detail: Although the paper provides concrete resource estimates (Q# compilation-style counts) showing substantial savings using QSP and gives numerical thresholds (≈4.7k logical qubits, ≈2.4×10^9 T-gates at ≈45 MHz), these claims are based on compiled-resource simulation assumptions (not demonstration on hardware) and on application-specific assumptions (benchmark instance, error model, classical baseline 1s). As a preprint, the asserted feasibility of 'quantum advantage' is therefore speculative pending hardware realization and broader validation.
limitations: QSP method in current form only provides approximations to single-variable functions (author-stated)
QSP transformations considered are restricted to functions with definite parity (even or odd) and the operational domain/range is limited to [0,1] (author-stated)
This work focuses specifically on the payoff component of derivative pricing and does not replace quantum arithmetic in other parts of the pipeline (author-stated)

Resource estimates are provided for a particular problem instance and choice of parameters (a = 3 assets, T = 20 timesteps, n = 15, p = 5, target error ϵ = 2×10^-3); generalization to other problem sizes or precision levels is not demonstrated (inferred)
No experimental validation on physical quantum hardware; results are circuit constructions and resource estimates rather than hardware runs (inferred)

Resource estimates are given at the logical level and rely on assumptions about error correction, logical gate speeds and achievable T-gate rates (e.g., 45 MHz) — mapping to physical qubit counts and realistic fault-tolerant overheads is not fully detailed (inferred)

Reproducibility risk: code and complete implementation details are not fully described in the manuscript (although existing packages are cited), so reproducing end-to-end resource numbers may require access to the authors' extended Q# code or parameter choices (inferred)

QSP requires constructing polynomial approximations of sometimes high degree (e.g., d = 20 here); numerical stability and cost of computing phase factors for larger/harder functions may limit applicability (inferred)

Although QSP removes explicit exponentiation arithmetic, comparator/addition circuits (e.g., adding shift s, comparisons) are still required and carry their own resource costs which remain in the circuit (inferred)

The Usin-driven QSP variant incurs high T-depth because of many controlled-Ry rotations and the necessity to synthesize them to high precision — this creates a tradeoff and potential bottleneck (author-discussed / inferred)

The paper considers typical payoff forms (A e^x − B)/C; handling payoffs with discontinuities or non-differentiable features (e.g., certain digital payoffs) may be problematic or require additional preprocessing (inferred)

key_ideas: #idea:quantum-advantage — Using Quantum Signal Processing (QSP/QSVT) to encode payoffs into amplitudes avoids expensive coherent arithmetic and yields large reductions in T-count (≈16×) and logical qubits (≈4×) versus an arithmetic baseline for the studied instances.

#idea:quantum-advantage — The constructed Usqrt unitary (uniform superposition + comparator) composes with QSP polynomials to implement payoff-transformations (e.g. sqrt/composed functions) with lower Clifford+T resource costs than prior arithmetic/look-up approaches.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The end-to-end pipeline integrates classical polynomial optimization (Chebyshev/minimax) and classical iterative amplitude estimation (IQAE) with quantum circuits, demonstrating a practical hybrid protocol for derivative pricing resource estimation.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Detailed Clifford+T accounting (Toffoli decompositions, ripple-carry comparator costs) and Q# implementations produce end-to-end metrics (T-count, T-depth, logical qubits, implied logical T-gate rate) enabling direct comparison to prior methods.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The approach relies on classical toolkits (QSPPACK/pyqsp) to compute QSP phase factors and uses classical pre/post-processing (reparameterization and IQAE) to make the quantum components implementable and analyzable.
